messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mateo was 26, a divorced Latin American man who worked as a maid in other people’s homes, moving through apartments and office suites with cleaning carts and folded rags, trying to keep his head down and finish before anyone asked too many questions. He had been detained and tortured after being accused of helping the wrong people, and what stayed with him was not only the pain but the helplessness of being held while men in uniforms questioned him, struck him, and made him feel that his body was no longer his own. Since then, ordinary things had taken on the force of warning signs. A similar car easing slowly past his bus stop could jolt him back into the feeling that someone had found him. Related media content—news footage, crime shows, even a passing clip of men in uniforms on a phone screen—could leave him tense and withdrawn for the rest of the day. He also found himself confused by positive emotions; if a coworker laughed with him or someone showed him kindness, he would sometimes feel a strange unease, as if letting himself feel good made him careless and exposed.

Those reminders quickly shaped how Mateo moved through the world. If a family member brought up what had happened, or if a supervisor hovered too closely while giving instructions, he would shut down, change the subject, or leave the room. Being around authority figures or anyone in a uniform—security guards, police officers, even building managers—made him feel cornered, so he started choosing routes and shifts that reduced the chance of meeting them. He smoked throughout the day, telling himself it helped him get through the hours, and more than once he stepped outside to light a cigarette after seeing a car like the ones he associated with his detention. In those moments he was not simply trying to calm himself; he was also trying to regain a sense of control, to keep from being pulled into the memory and the fear it brought with it.

What frightened Mateo most was that the fear seemed to live in his body now. He woke in the night to check whether he was safe, sitting up and scanning the room before he could go back to sleep. In the daytime he reacted with alarm when someone touched him unexpectedly, flinching hard if a coworker brushed his shoulder in a narrow hallway or if a client tapped his arm to get his attention. Even in ordinary situations he felt threatened when strangers approached him, reading their movement too quickly and bracing for trouble before he knew what they wanted. Those same fears made his work harder. On cleaning jobs he became watchful in lobbies and parking lots, especially if a car idled nearby or someone in authority came into view, and he found himself checking exits before entering an apartment. The more he felt on guard, the more he sought out things that seemed to protect him in the moment: cigarettes, avoidance, staying away from reminders whenever possible.

But those efforts also kept the danger alive for him. Because he avoided reminders when others brought them up, he never had much chance to settle after a trigger or to discover that the moment would pass; instead, every mention of the event felt like proof that it was still close. His habit of steering clear of authority figures and uniforms narrowed his world at work, sometimes forcing him to take jobs farther from home or to let a supervisor speak through another employee, which made him feel more dependent and vulnerable. Smoking became one of the few things he could do quickly when his body went tight, but it also left him more tied to the pattern of scanning, stepping outside, and watching the street for the next similar car. Positive moments could be the hardest to trust: if he let himself relax with someone, the sudden openness seemed to make the next alarm sharper, and he would pull back before he could feel fully at ease.

Over months, Mateo’s life had become organized around these reactions. The same triggers that once appeared as isolated shocks now seemed to recruit the next wave of fear, and the fear kept sending him back to the habits that narrowed his life further. He finally sought help after a week in which he woke repeatedly to check the doors, flinched badly when a client touched his arm, and then spent the rest of the day avoiding his supervisor because the man wore a city maintenance uniform. He said he was most afraid that he would keep living as though the torture were still happening, but he also hoped that he might someday ride past a similar car, hear a story about what happened, or feel something good without his whole body going rigid.
